edition: Issue 049: England hand the All Blacks their biggest demolition ever, Westpac declares Black Friday a myth (with charts), and the voters ask for a menu with more than two options
tagline: Your 3-minute Sunday reset: the record loss that made 1998 feel recent, the bank debunking retail's loudest weekend, and New Zealand's great political appetite, reviewed by the man who called it 'shit food'.

stories.headline: England put 37-12 on the All Blacks — a record loss to England, a five-loss season, and a 3:10am history lesson
stories.summary: England ran in five tries to beat the All Blacks 37-12 at Twickenham — the heaviest defeat New Zealand have ever suffered against England and their fifth test loss of the year (first time since 1998), with coach Dave Rennie and his staff now under enormous pressure before next weekend's playoff.

body.text: England ran in five tries to beat the All Blacks 37-12 at Twickenham early Sunday morning (NZT) — the heaviest defeat New Zealand have ever suffered against England, and their fifth test loss of the year, the first time they've lost five in a season since 1998. RNZ's match report called the performance 'lethargic and disconnected': the set piece was poor, discipline again below the required standard, the defence the worst since last year's hiding in Wellington, and the attack 'error-ridden and toothless'. England were over inside five minutes through Henry Slade and never looked back; No.8 Ben Earl, deservedly man of the match, scored an individual try from an attacking scrum. Captain Codie Taylor's verdict: 'We were just really inaccurate tonight.' The 25-point margin is the largest in All Blacks–England history, the five losses match the All Blacks' worst season of the professional era (NZ Herald), and the Nations Championship's No.1 Southern Hemisphere seeding and playoff spot is now effectively South Africa's to lose. Dave Rennie and his coaching staff face enormous pressure to salvage something from the playoff next weekend.

Right, deep breath, because this is now a national coping exercise and we're all in it together. The record loss to England — 25 points, their biggest margin over us, ever — arrived at 3:10am New Zealand time, which the schedulers clearly chose because they wanted to test how committed our suffering actually is. It's the fifth loss of a year now officially the worst of the professional era, and when the autopsy points at 'the quality of the advice the players are receiving from their coaches', that's rugby code for a group chat with no new ideas and nobody willing to say it. Here's the truly magnificent part: there is another playoff next weekend — an encore nobody requested, likely at another ungodly hour — and we will absolutely be there, bleary-eyed, wearing the jersey, because we're wonderful at catastrophising and terrible at walking away. Enjoy the ride, everyone. At least it's not 1949. Yet.

RNZ (22 Nov 2026, Patrick McKendry, 'All Blacks humbled in record loss to England'): England scored five tries in a 37-12 win at Twickenham; the 25-point margin was the All Blacks' largest ever against England; it was New Zealand's fifth test loss of 2026, the first time they have lost five in a year since 1998 (they lost six in 1949); the set piece was poor, discipline not up to standard, the defensive display their worst since South Africa beat them in Wellington last year; the All Blacks lost four lineouts on their own throw; Henry Slade scored inside five minutes (grubber from Fin Smith), Jack van Portvliet and Ben Earl (man of the match) also crossed; captain Codie Taylor: 'We were just really inaccurate tonight'; questions remain over 'the quality of the advice the players are receiving from their coaches'; the No.1 Southern Hemisphere seeding and a top playoff spot are now South Africa's to lose (they play Ireland in Dublin), with the All Blacks' playoff opponent still to be decided. RNZ (20 Nov 2026, Joe Porter): the test kicked off at 3:10am NZT at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham. NZ Herald (21 Nov 2026, 'We were miles off': Rennie owns All Blacks' record loss): five losses equal the All Blacks' worst season of the professional era.

stories.headline: 'Nothing special' about Black Friday, says Westpac — 30-40 percent of appliances are 'discounted' all year round
stories.summary: Westpac's analysis of Stats NZ data finds bargains all year round — 30-40 percent of household appliances discounted in any quarter, similar average savings outside December — while its own card data shows Black Friday spending last year still ran 48 percent higher than a typical Friday.

body.text: Black Friday is six days away (Friday 27 November) and the bank has spoilt the party early. Westpac's analysis of Stats NZ data found 30-40 percent of household appliances are available discounted all year round, and the average size of those discounts is not always larger in the December quarter than in any other. About 18 percent of clothing items were discounted every quarter — with similar average savings through the year — and about 36 percent of furnishings were discounted every quarter. The bank's own card data concedes the event still has pull: Black Friday spending last year was 48 percent higher than a typical Friday (up from a 43 percent jump in 2024), transactions for appliances tripled, and recreation equipment and shoe purchases doubled. 'There are certainly bargains out there,' said Westpac product, sustainability and marketing managing director Sarah Hearn, 'but our analysis of Stats NZ data shows that bargains come around more often than you might think.' Her advice: know what you want and what you're prepared to pay — and if 'that one last purchase is pushing you too far into debt, take a step back'. Financial wellbeing programme manager Warren Ngan Woo suggests price-matching apps and warns that Christmas shopping creates FOMO.

A bank, of all institutions, has stepped in to tell us the sale to end all sales is, statistically, just a Friday. Let it land: appliances are 'discounted' 30 to 40 percent of the year, which is a polite way of saying the recommended retail price is a fiction the marketing department prints, and the sale is the real price wearing a party hat. The emails screaming THIS IS YOUR LAST CHANCE have now been wrong forty-seven Fridays in a row, and Westpac — the same people who charge you to hold the money they're advising you not to spend — has concluded the FOMO is the actual product. The bank's advice, translated: 'do your own market research' is corporate for 'trust no one, including us'. Still, the oven needs to be replaced, and it might as well happen during the one week of the year when the discount sign must legally justify its own existence. Write the budget down, buy the thing, mute the emails, and enjoy your purchases 48-percent-of-a-typical-Friday-free.

RNZ (22 Nov 2026, Susan Edmunds, 'Nothing special about Black Friday deals — Westpac'): the bank's analysis of Stats NZ data found it common for 30-40 percent of household appliances to be available discounted all year round, with the average discount size not always larger in the December quarter than in any other; about 18 percent of clothing items were discounted every quarter with average discounts similar through the year; about 36 percent of furnishing items were discounted every quarter; Westpac card data: Black Friday spending last year was 48 percent higher than a typical Friday, versus a 43 percent rise in 2024; transactions for appliances tripled on Black Friday, while recreation equipment and shoe purchases were double the normal level; quotes from managing director Sarah Hearn ('bargains come around more often than you might think', 'know what they want to buy and how much they're prepared to spend', 'if that one last purchase is pushing you too far into debt, take a step back') and financial wellbeing programme manager Warren Ngan Woo (price-matching apps, FOMO at Christmas, 'you have to do your own market research'). Black Friday 2026 falls on Friday 27 November in New Zealand, with Cyber Monday on Monday 30 November (public holiday calendars and NZ retailer schedules, checked 22 Nov 2026).

stories.headline: 'Picking which shit food to eat': the voters explain why National and Labour both sit on 29 percent
stories.summary: RNZ's Focus on Politics asks whether New Zealanders are sick of politics or sick of politicians, with turnout at this election on track to be its second lowest in history and both major parties on 29 percent on preliminary results — one West Auckland voter likened the choice to 'picking which shit food to eat' and voted for nobody.

body.text: Are New Zealanders sick of politics — or just sick of politicians? That is the question at the heart of RNZ's latest Focus on Politics feature, published with turnout at this election 'on track to be its second lowest in history' and both major parties on 29 percent on preliminary results, after polling in the low thirties and even twenties all year. One West Auckland voter told RNZ that choosing between the parties felt like 'picking which shit food to eat' — and chose not to vote for anyone. Another Aucklander: 'All of these empty promises, all the time, saying things are going to happen and then they just don't happen.' The feature gathers the trends RNZ tracked through the campaign — a rise in threats towards MPs, negative campaigning surging since 2020, and sexist and racist abuse in politics — and asks whether the 'attention economy' is making the cynicism worse. Former chief science advisor Sir Peter Gluckman describes the drift away from both majors as the 'hollowing out' of the political middle; international relations academic Reuben Steff, now at Mendel University in the Czech Republic, frames it as part of a global crisis of confidence in democracy, amplified by algorithms that reward outrage.

The 'picking which shit food to eat' guy deserves the widest possible platform and probably a doctorate. Stand-up philosophers will study him; coalition negotiators should send him a fruit basket, because he has articulated the national mood better than any 60-second ad of this entire campaign. Both major parties are on 29 percent, which in school terms is a C-minus with 'must do better on the homework promises' written in the margin — and the voters' review is harsher than any teacher's: 'empty promises, all the time, saying things are going to happen and then they just don't happen.' The experts have big words for it — the hollowing out of the political middle, a global crisis of confidence in democracy — and the voters have their own words for it, and they can't be printed on the front page. To the politicians who read the papers on Sunday morning: the electorate isn't tuning out of democracy, it's asking for a menu with more than two items, and it's noticed the specials keep being lies. Also — 29 percent is not a mandate, it's a participation award with a threat attached.

RNZ (22 Nov 2026, Lillian Hanly, 'Are New Zealanders sick of politics — or sick of politicians?'): this election's voter turnout is on track to be its second lowest in history; National and Labour were each on 29 percent on preliminary results after consistently polling in the low thirties and even twenties through the year, with the two major parties combined at historic lows; a West Auckland voter likened choosing between the parties to 'picking which shit food to eat' and chose not to vote for anyone; another Aucklander spoke of 'empty promises'; RNZ's campaign coverage tracked a rise in threats towards MPs, negative campaigning surging since 2020, and sexist and racist abuse in politics; Sir Peter Gluckman described the trend as the 'hollowing out' of the political middle; Reuben Steff (associate professor, Mendel University, Czech Republic) links it to a global crisis of confidence in democracy — distrust of political institutions, populist sentiment, media distrust, disinformation and declining civic skills, with social-media algorithms amplifying outrage and shorter attention spans undermining informed debate.
